headline: SMSF succession planning is critical: cognitive decline, death and incapacity create structural and legal risks trustees must prepare for while still capable
reasoning: Ben Graham-Nellor discusses the real-world risks facing SMSF trustees as they age, including cognitive decline, death of a member, and the legal complexity of transferring trustee responsibilities. He notes that enduring powers of attorney do not automatically confer trustee status, and that a formal appointment process must occur. The ATO allows six months to restructure a fund following a member's death. He emphasises that binding death benefit nominations are essential because superannuation is not automatically an estate asset dealt with via a will. His key advice is to simplify the SMSF and put succession structures in place while all members still have full capacity.
quote: So there's a couple of things to think about South. All members of the supplemented super fund should know a few things about it. Now, quite often you do find that one member of the fund is, is kind of the chief financial officer of the fund, if you like, who's looking after everything to do with it. They know when the tax is due, they know when the audit's happening, they're paying the all the bills out of the fund. And then maybe one or two or three of the other members don't really take an active role. But it's very important that everybody understands a few things about their funds. First of all, who is the trustee? Do you have an individual trustee structure or corporate trustee structure? Because that makes a difference at the end of the day if you have to. If you have a member pass away or become incapable of running the fund, looking at who has power of attorney over the members of the fund as well. And, and remembering that holding an enduring power between it doesn't automatically make somebody else the trustee if they take over from you. But then we need to have that process in place. It's important for everyone to know who's getting the benefit, the binding death dominations, how that all works when someone was to pass away and what's going to happen to the assets within the fund.
episode_title: The SMSF risks trustees need to plan for | the advisory

headline: Ben Graham-Nellor flags AI, intergenerational wealth transfer, and changing consumer expectations as the three structural forces reshaping how Australians build and manage wealth over the next decade.
reasoning: Graham-Nellor identifies three macro-level structural forces affecting Australian wealth management: (1) AI making financial information universally accessible and shifting the adviser role from administrator to behavioural coach; (2) the great wealth transfer already underway, with JP Morgan estimating ~$5 trillion passing from baby boomers to younger generations by 2034; and (3) changing consumer expectations driven by those two forces. He argues that while AI improves financial literacy, human judgement becomes more valuable — not less — as information abundance grows. The intersection of AI and wealth transfer means the advice industry must adapt to serve a new, predominantly female client base.
quote: I think there's three structural forces that we're paying attention to at the moment. And the big one is artificial intelligence and how that is affecting people and their money and how they seek advice about their money. The second course is the great wealth transfer, which is which is already started and going to be taking place over the next decade. And then that brings in the third, which is changing consumer expectations.
episode_title: Why advisers need to rethink the next generation of wealth | the advisory

headline: Ben Graham-Nellor highlights that women are expected to inherit ~65% of Australia's $5 trillion intergenerational wealth transfer by 2034, fundamentally shifting who leads family wealth conversations.
reasoning: Graham-Nellor cites JP Morgan estimates of nearly $5 trillion in wealth passing between generations in Australia by 2034, with women expected to receive approximately 65% (~$3.2 trillion) of that transfer. This is described as the largest intergenerational wealth transfer ever seen in Australia. The implication is that family wealth conversations will increasingly be led by women as custodians of capital, and the financial advice industry — where only ~22% of advisers are women — must adapt its service model accordingly. He notes women clients tend to ask 'will I be okay?' rather than 'can I do better?', preferring conversations around financial security, long-term planning, family outcomes, and values-based goals.
quote: JP, where estimates there's nearly about $5 trillion passed from sort of baby boomers and their parents down to the next generations by 2034. So we're already, doing that. It's already underway, and it's the largest intergenerational wealth transfer that we've ever seen in Australia. And for the first time, women are expected to receive about 65% of that transfer. So they're going to inherit the majority of that money, or about $3.2 trillion. And what that means for the future is that family wealth conversations are going to be led more by women than by the men, as the women are are custodians of that capital.
episode_title: Why advisers need to rethink the next generation of wealth | the advisory

headline: Ben Graham-Nellor argues AI will make financial advice more human by freeing advisers from administration, but warns that clients relying solely on AI tools like ChatGPT risk acting on hallucinated or incorrect financial information.
reasoning: Graham-Nellor notes the most common current use of AI among financial advisers is transcribing and summarising meeting notes, freeing up time for deeper client conversations. He argues this shifts the adviser role toward behavioural coaching rather than administration. However, he cautions that AI tools like ChatGPT have already given incorrect advice to clients in his practice, and that entering personal financial details into AI systems carries privacy and strategic risks. He concludes that AI should complement, not replace, professional advice.
quote: We've had two clients come to us and and ask us questions about the advice that we've given them based on what ChatGPT told them. And in both situations, ChatGPT had that wrong. So it's very important to remember that, um, AI's can't hallucinate. Um, and it's also always worth checking in with a professional at the same time... the main way that advisors are using AI at the moment, the most common way, I should say is, for writing notes. Um, recording meetings, having notes. Um summarized by AI in order to spend more time actually just talking to clients. Um, I think that having AI involved in a financial advice process is actually going to make the advice more human.
episode_title: Why advisers need to rethink the next generation of wealth | the advisory

headline: Intergenerational wealth transfer to women will reshape financial advice industry in Australia
reasoning: Ben Graham-Nellor notes that only about 22% of financial advisors in Australia are women, yet the coming intergenerational wealth transfer will see wealth inherited predominantly by women. He argues that female clients prefer conversations around financial security, long-term planning, family outcomes, caregiving impacts, and values-based advice rather than pure investment returns. Advisors accustomed to male-dominated client bases will need to shift their approach to participate in this wealth transfer. He also highlights the need for more women to enter the financial advice profession to better serve this demographic shift.
quote: Women are more likely to ask, you know, will I be okay than can I do better? The conversations that we find are preferred by our female clients are around financial security, longer term planning, family outcomes, caregiving impacts, and values based advice. And advisors who are used to dealing with men in a very male dominated industry are going to have to start thinking beyond investments and returns if they want to take part in that wealth transfer that's already started.
episode_title: Why advisers need to rethink the next generation of wealth | the advisory

headline: AI can assist wealth education for inheritance recipients but carries hallucination and privacy risks
reasoning: Ben Graham-Nellor sees AI as a useful educational tool for Australians expecting to inherit significant wealth, allowing them to research investment markets and ask questions. However, he cautions that AI does not have the full picture, can hallucinate with incorrect answers, and poses privacy risks if personal details are entered into free-tier services that use data for model training. He recommends using paid AI services with appropriate data protections.
quote: You can you can get asked lots of questions. You can, um, you can research money, how investment markets work. And if you're someone that knows an inheritance is coming and you're not used to dealing with those kind of levels of money financially, educating yourself is so important. Um, we always have to remember, though, with AI that it doesn't have the full picture and it sometimes does hallucinate and gives answers that can just be crazy. And it's also always worth remembering that if you're putting your personal details into AI, you need to make sure that one you're paying for that, and you've made sure that those personal details are not being spread, um, to around the place to for the AI to learn off.
episode_title: Why advisers need to rethink the next generation of wealth | the advisory
